valid-parentheses.pattern: Stack of open brackets (the most recent opener must close first)

approaches.name: Keep deleting matched pairs
approaches.idea: A valid string always contains an adjacent pair `()`, `[]` or `{}` somewhere. Delete such pairs until none is left; the string was valid exactly when it ends up empty.
steps: Repeat: replace every `()`, `[]` and `{}` with nothing.
Stop when a round removes nothing.
Return whether the string is now empty.
approaches.why: Each round is O(n) and removes at least one pair, so up to n/2 rounds. Each round builds a new string.

approaches.name: Stack of expected closers
approaches.idea: Read left to right. Every opening bracket must be closed before any bracket opened earlier, which is last-in-first-out order: push what each opener expects, and check each closer against the top of the stack.
steps: For each character: if it is an opener, push its matching closer.
If it is a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must equal this character; pop it, otherwise return false.
At the end, return whether the stack is empty (no opener left unclosed).
approaches.why: One push or pop per character; the stack holds up to n openers (e.g. `((((`).

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.pattern: Stack as the output buffer (compare each character with the top)

approaches.name: Remove one adjacent pair at a time
approaches.idea: Simulate the rule literally: find any two equal neighbours, delete them, and start again until no pair is left.
steps: Scan for the first index `i` with `s[i] == s[i + 1]`.
If found, remove those two characters and scan again from just before them.
When no pair is found, return the string.
approaches.why: Up to n/2 removals, each costing O(n) to rebuild the string. For n = 10⁵ this is too slow.

approaches.name: Stack: cancel against the last kept character
approaches.idea: Build the answer left to right. A new character either cancels the last kept character (if they are equal) or is kept. Cancelling can expose an older character, which is exactly what a stack handles.
steps: Use a string builder as a stack.
For each character: if the builder is non-empty and its last character equals it, delete that last character; otherwise append it.
Return the builder's contents.
approaches.why: Each character is pushed once and popped at most once; the builder holds up to n characters (the output).

backspace-string-compare.pattern: Stack simulation, or two pointers from the end that skip deleted characters

approaches.name: Build both final texts with a stack
approaches.idea: Type each string into a stack: a letter is pushed, `#` pops (if anything is there). Compare the two results.
steps: For each string, push letters and pop on `#` when the stack is not empty.
Turn both stacks into strings.
Return whether they are equal.
approaches.why: One pass per string; the two stacks hold up to n + m characters.

approaches.name: Two pointers from the end
approaches.idea: A `#` only affects characters before it, so read both strings backwards. Keep a count of pending backspaces and skip the characters they delete; then compare the next surviving character of each string.
steps: Set `i` and `j` at the last index of `s` and `t`.
Move `i` left to the next surviving character: a `#` adds one to `skip`; a letter with `skip > 0` uses one up; otherwise stop. Do the same for `j`.
If both are in range, the characters must be equal; if exactly one is in range, return false; if neither, return true.
Step both left and repeat.
approaches.why: Each index is passed once; only the two indices and two skip counters are stored.

evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.pattern: Operand stack (an operator pops its two operands and pushes the result)

approaches.name: Repeatedly collapse the first operator
approaches.idea: The first operator in the list always applies to the two values just before it. Replace those three tokens with their result and repeat until one value remains.
steps: Copy the tokens into a list.
Find the first operator at index `i`; compute `list[i − 2] op list[i − 1]`.
Replace the three tokens with the result; repeat until one token is left, and return it.
approaches.why: Each of up to n/2 operators needs a scan and a list removal, both O(n).

approaches.name: One pass with a stack
approaches.idea: Push numbers. An operator applies to the two most recent values: pop the right operand, then the left, and push the result. The last value on the stack is the answer.
steps: For each token: if it is a number, push it.
If it is an operator: pop `b`, then pop `a`, and push `a op b` (the order matters for `-` and `/`).
Division truncates toward zero.
Return the single value left on the stack.
approaches.why: One push or pop per token; the stack holds up to about n/2 numbers.

asteroid-collision.pattern: Stack of survivors (a left-mover collides with right-movers on top of the stack)

approaches.name: Resolve one collision at a time
approaches.idea: A collision happens only where a right-mover is immediately followed by a left-mover. Find such a pair, resolve it, and repeat until none is left.
steps: Keep the asteroids in a list.
Find the first `i` with `a[i] > 0` and `a[i + 1] < 0`.
Remove the smaller one, or both if equal sizes; repeat until no such pair exists.
Return the list.
approaches.why: Each collision removes at least one asteroid (at most n collisions), and each search and removal is O(n).

approaches.name: Stack of survivors
approaches.idea: Process asteroids left to right, keeping the survivors so far on a stack. Only a left-mover arriving while right-movers are on top can collide, so it fights the top until it is destroyed or nothing on top moves right.
steps: For each asteroid `x`: set `alive = true`.
While `alive`, `x < 0`, and the top of the stack is positive: if `top < −x`, pop it and keep going; if `top == −x`, pop it and `x` dies too; if `top > −x`, `x` dies.
If `x` is still alive, push it.
The stack, bottom to top, is the answer.
approaches.why: Every asteroid is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so all the while loops together do O(n) work.

simplify-path.pattern: Stack of directory names (".." pops, "." and empty parts are ignored)

approaches.name: Split on "/" and keep a stack of directories
approaches.idea: Split the path into parts. Each real name goes deeper (push); `..` goes up one level (pop, if not at the root); `.` and the empty parts made by repeated slashes do nothing. The stack is the canonical path.
steps: Split `path` on `/`.
For each part: skip it if it is empty or `.`; if it is `..`, pop when the stack is non-empty; otherwise push it.
Join the stack with `/` and put one `/` in front (the root alone is `/`).
approaches.why: Splitting and joining are linear in the path length; the parts and the stack hold O(n) characters. There is no slower approach worth writing: every character must be read once anyway.

basic-calculator-ii.pattern: Stack of signed terms (apply * and / immediately, add everything at the end)

approaches.name: Stack of terms
approaches.idea: Read each number together with the operator before it. `+x` and `−x` start a new term (push `x` or `−x`); `*x` and `/x` change the last term (pop, combine, push). The answer is the sum of the stack.
steps: Keep `num = 0` and `op = "+"` (the operator before the current number).

For each character: digits extend `num`. When a non-space operator or the end of the string is reached, apply `op` to `num`: push `num` for `+`, `−num` for `−`, or pop and push `top * num` / `top / num` (truncating toward zero) for `*` and `/`.
Then remember the new operator as `op` and reset `num`.
Return the sum of the stack.
approaches.why: One pass over the string; the stack holds one entry per `+`/`−` term, up to O(n).

approaches.name: Running total plus the last term
approaches.idea: Only the most recent term can still be changed by `*` or `/`; everything before it is final. So keep `total` (finished terms) and `last` (the current term) instead of a whole stack.
steps: Keep `total = 0`, `last = 0`, `num = 0`, `op = "+"`.
When an operator or the end is reached: for `+`/`−`, add `last` to `total` and set `last = ±num`; for `*`/`/`, set `last = last * num` or `last / num` (truncating toward zero).
Then remember the new operator and reset `num`.
Return `total + last`.
approaches.why: One pass; four variables replace the stack.

decode-string.pattern: Stack of (partial string, repeat count) for nested brackets

approaches.name: Recursive descent
approaches.idea: Decoding `k[...]` means decoding the inside first. A recursive function reads characters from a shared index until it meets `]` (or the end), and calls itself for every nested `k[`.
steps: Keep a shared index `i`. `decode()` builds a result string.
While `i` is in range and `s[i] != "]"`: a letter is appended; digits are read into `k`, then skip `[`, call `decode()` for the inside, skip `]`, and append the inside `k` times.
Return the result; the top-level call decodes the whole string.
approaches.why: Each input character is read once, and the work of copying is proportional to the output length L. The recursion depth is at most the nesting depth (≤ n), plus the output itself.

approaches.name: Explicit stack of (text so far, count)
approaches.idea: The same idea without recursion. On `[`, save the text built so far and the repeat count, and start a fresh piece. On `]`, the fresh piece is complete: repeat it and append it to the saved text.
steps: Keep `cur` (text being built) and `k` (number being read), plus two stacks.
Digit: `k = k * 10 + digit`. Letter: append to `cur`.
`[`: push `cur` and `k`, then reset both.
`]`: pop `prev` and `count`; set `cur = prev + cur repeated count`. Return `cur` at the end.
approaches.why: Same work as the recursive version: each character is read once and the copying is proportional to the output length L. The stacks hold at most one entry per nesting level.

longest-valid-parentheses.pattern: Stack of indices with a "last unmatched" base, or two counter scans

approaches.name: Check every even-length substring
approaches.idea: Test every substring with a balance counter; keep the longest that is well-formed.
steps: For each start `i`, walk `j` to the right keeping `balance` (+1 for `(`, −1 for `)`).
If `balance` drops below 0, no longer substring from `i` can be valid: stop.
Whenever `balance == 0`, `s[i..j]` is valid: update the best with `j − i + 1`.
approaches.why: n starts, each scanning up to n characters. (Checking each substring from scratch would be O(n³); extending the balance avoids that.)

approaches.name: Stack of indices
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of indices whose bottom is the last position that cannot be part of a valid run (start with −1). A `)` pops its matching `(`; the valid run ending here then starts right after the new top.
steps: Push −1.
For each `i`: if `s[i] == "("`, push `i`.
Otherwise pop. If the stack is now empty, this `)` is unmatched: push `i` as the new base. Otherwise update the best with `i − top`.
Return the best.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed and popped at most once; the stack can hold up to n indices.

approaches.name: Two scans with open/close counters
approaches.idea: Scanning left to right, count `(` and `)`. Equal counts mean a valid run; more `)` than `(` means the run is broken, so reset. This misses runs with extra `(` (like `(()`), so scan right to left too with the roles swapped.
steps: Left to right: count `open` and `close`. If equal, update the best with `2·close`; if `close > open`, reset both to 0.
Right to left: same, but update when equal and reset when `open > close`.
Return the best.
approaches.why: Two linear scans with two counters. Every valid run is caught by one of the two scans: a left-to-right scan only fails when there are unmatched `(` before the run ends, and those are exactly the cases the reverse scan handles.

approaches.name: List with removals at the end
approaches.idea: Keep the scores in a plain list, look back by index, and recompute the total at the end.
steps: For each operation, append, double, add the last two, or delete the last element of the list.
Sum the list at the end.
approaches.why: A dynamic list used only at its end already behaves like a stack, so this is linear too. It is the same idea with less explicit structure.

approaches.name: Stack with a running total
approaches.idea: Push scores on a stack and keep the total up to date as you go, so no final pass is needed.
steps: For a number, push it and add it to `total`. For "D", push twice the top and add it.
For "+", pop the top `a`, peek `b`, push `a` back, push `a + b` and add it.
For "C", pop the top and subtract it. Return `total`.
approaches.why: Each operation is O(1). Only the most recent scores are ever read, which is exactly what a stack provides, and "C" is a pop. The stack can hold up to n scores.

car-fleet.pattern: Sort by position, then a monotonic stack of arrival times

approaches.name: Check every car ahead
approaches.idea: A car leads a fleet exactly when no car in front of it arrives later (or at the same time) on its own. Check that for each car by scanning all the others.
steps: Compute each car's solo time `t[i] = (target − position[i]) / speed[i]`.
Car `i` starts a fleet if no car `j` with `position[j] > position[i]` has `t[j] >= t[i]`.
Count such cars.
approaches.why: If some car ahead is no faster to arrive, car `i` catches it (or the fleet it is in) before or at `target`. Otherwise car `i` is never blocked. Correct, but 10¹⁰ checks for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Sort, then a stack of fleet times
approaches.idea: Visit cars from the closest to `target` backwards. Push each car's solo time; if it is not more than the fleet time on top of the stack, the car merges into that fleet and is popped again.
steps: Pair each position with its speed and sort by position, descending.
For each car compute its time `t`. If the stack is not empty and `t <=` the top, the car catches that fleet and merges: skip it. Otherwise push `t` as a new fleet.
The stack size is the number of fleets.
approaches.why: A merged car takes on the fleet's (slower) time, so only each fleet's leading time matters. The stack is strictly increasing from bottom to top, which is the monotonic-stack shape.

approaches.name: Bucket by position, keep only the slowest time
approaches.idea: Positions are integers below `target`, so place each car in an array indexed by position instead of sorting. Then sweep from `target` down, keeping just the time of the fleet in front.
steps: Make `time[p]` for `p` in `[0, target)`, filled with 0, and set `time[position[i]]` to car `i`'s solo time.
Sweep `p` from `target − 1` down to 0 with `slowest = 0`.
When `time[p] > slowest`, a new fleet starts: count it and set `slowest = time[p]`.
approaches.why: Counting-sort by position removes the log factor; it is a win when `target` is not much larger than n (here up to 10⁶). The stack is replaced by one variable, because a new fleet only ever compares with the fleet directly ahead. Equal times merge (`>` not `>=`), matching "catches up exactly at target".
